name: Nabothian cyst
aliases: mucinous retention cyst of the cervix

reference.source: Standard gynaecology textbook and colposcopy guidance
clinicalPearls: A nabothian cyst is a benign mucus-filled retention cyst on the cervix formed when the opening of an endocervical gland becomes covered by squamous epithelium during normal metaplasia
They are extremely common, usually multiple, and almost always asymptomatic incidental findings on speculum examination or pelvic imaging
Typical appearance is one or more smooth, translucent or yellowish-white raised nodules on the ectocervix, often over the transformation zone
They require no treatment when characteristic and asymptomatic, and reassurance is the mainstay of management
On ultrasound they appear as well-defined cystic spaces within the cervix and can occasionally be large or deep, prompting unnecessary concern if misinterpreted
Rarely, very large or numerous deep cysts (so-called tunnel clusters) can be mistaken on imaging for a cervical neoplasm, so correlation with the benign clinical picture is important
Intervention such as marsupialisation or excision is only considered if a cyst is unusually large, symptomatic, or the diagnosis is uncertain
Cervical screening should continue as normal, since nabothian cysts themselves carry no malignant potential
reference.pathophysiology: The cervix undergoes continuous squamous metaplasia at the transformation zone, where columnar endocervical epithelium is progressively replaced by squamous epithelium. When advancing squamous epithelium grows over the mouth of a mucus-secreting endocervical gland, the gland's outflow is obstructed and mucus is retained, distending it into a smooth cyst. The process is entirely physiological and benign, and the cysts have no relationship to infection or malignancy. Their main clinical relevance is avoiding misdiagnosis, since deep or clustered cysts can superficially resemble other cervical lesions on imaging.
additionalDifferentials: Mesonephric or other benign cervical cyst
Adenoma malignum or minimal-deviation adenocarcinoma (rare, when deep cysts are atypical)
additionalInvestigations: Speculum examination to identify characteristic smooth cervical cysts
Transvaginal ultrasound where imaging characterisation is needed
Colposcopy if the appearance is atypical or screening is abnormal
Magnetic resonance imaging for unusually large or deep cystic lesions to reassure and exclude neoplasia
Cervical cytology and human papillomavirus testing as part of routine screening
redFlags: Atypical, rapidly enlarging, or irregular cervical lesion that could represent malignancy
Abnormal bleeding, particularly postcoital or postmenopausal, warranting further assessment
Deep or extensive cystic change on imaging that raises the question of adenoma malignum
reference.prognosis: Nabothian cysts are benign with an excellent prognosis, requiring no treatment in the vast majority of cases and carrying no risk of malignant transformation.
pitfalls: Over-investigating or excising a characteristic asymptomatic cyst unnecessarily
Misinterpreting deep or clustered cysts on imaging as cervical malignancy
Attributing abnormal bleeding to a nabothian cyst and failing to exclude other cervical pathology
Neglecting routine cervical screening because a benign cyst is present
references: Standard gynaecology reference text on benign cervical lesions
management: Reassure that the lesion is a benign mucus-retention cyst requiring no treatment when the appearance is characteristic and asymptomatic
Confirm the benign nature on speculum examination and correlate with routine cervical screening cytology and human papillomavirus testing
Reserve transvaginal ultrasound or MRI for unusually large, deep or clustered (tunnel-cluster) cysts to distinguish them from cervical neoplasia
Perform colposcopy if the appearance is atypical or screening is abnormal
Consider marsupialisation, electrocautery or excision only in the rare symptomatic case with discomfort or discharge
Avoid unnecessary intervention or over-investigation once the benign diagnosis is secure
